script.opening: (Nervous, defensive, speaking from her bedroom with headphones in.) "I need help and I really don't want a lecture. I'm 16, I'm pregnant — I did a test, it's positive — and I've thought about it a lot. I want an abortion. Please don't tell my mum, she'd kill me. Can you just sort it out for me, or am I too young to decide?"

facts.text: Last period "about seven weeks ago, I think". "No pain or bleeding." Feels sick in the mornings. Positive home test 4 days ago.
"I'm sure. It's my decision. Nobody's making me." Has thought about it for a week. Wants to finish her A-levels. Has not told anyone except her best friend.
If asked: "He's around my age. Yeah, it was what I wanted. It's not like that." Boyfriend Callum, 17, at the same college; together 8 months. Sex was consensual. He knows and supports her decision.
"No, nothing like that. Home's fine. Mum would just go mad." Lives with Mum and younger brother. No social worker. No one has hurt her. Not using drugs; drinks occasionally at parties.
Was using condoms, "one split, I think". Has never had an STI test. Interested in the implant: "Yeah, the implant maybe. And the test is fine."
Well. No medicines, no allergies, no previous pregnancies. No mental health problems; feels stressed but not low.
"My mobile. Text is best." Mum sometimes looks at post.
"That someone would say no, or make me feel like a bad person. And her finding out."

Wary and ready to be judged. Relaxes a lot if the doctor is warm, doesn't lecture and explains she can decide for herself: "Really? I thought you'd have to ring her." If the doctor moralises or pushes her to tell Mum, become short and say "Forget it." On involving Mum: "Maybe. I'll think about it." Asks: "Will they tell my mum?" and "Can you do it? I don't want to mess it up."

ice.ideas: "I want an abortion — but I don't know if I'm allowed to decide at 16."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — being judged or refused, and her mum finding out; scared of "messing up" the process.
ice.expectations: "For you to sort it out, privately."

cues: "I really don't want a lecture." — needs a non-judgemental tone.
"Please don't tell my mum." — explain confidentiality clearly.
"Am I too young to decide?" — invites explaining her right to consent.

checkpoints.text: Provides NON-JUDGEMENTAL, patient-centred care with ZERO editorialising about abortion, her age or her decision — centring her autonomy regardless of personal views

Assesses and AFFIRMS competence — at 16 presumed able to consent (Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8; Gillick competence for under-16s, Fraser only for contraception advice) — and answers clearly that she can decide without parental consent if competent
Respects CONFIDENTIALITY — encourages but does not force parental/trusted-adult involvement, and explains when/why confidentiality might be breached — building trust
Weaves in a SAFEGUARDING screen sensitively (father’s identity/age, consent to sex, coercion/CSE/grooming indicators, pressure about the decision) without making her feel policed

Gives BALANCED information on options without steering, refers PROMPTLY to abortion services or gives the self-referral route (time-critical; NICE NG140; QS199: abortion offered within 1 week of assessment; home early medical abortion up to 9 weeks 6 days), and addresses contraception and STI screening
Reads the fear of judgement and of her mother, makes her feel safe, believed and in control, and avoids any moral lecture
Explains confidentiality and competence in reassuring, accessible terms so she trusts the process

Safety-nets and follows up: clear plan and timing, ectopic red flags (one-sided or shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, fainting → 999/A&E), who to contact, contraception/STI follow-up, and any safeguarding action taken proportionately — competent, confidential, non-judgemental care

worked.txt: "No lecture — I promise. You’ve come to exactly the right place, and my job is to help you, not to judge you. Let’s take it at your pace."
"To your question — no, you’re not too young to decide. At 16 you’re allowed to make this decision for yourself, as long as you understand it, and from talking to you, you clearly do."

"I won’t tell your mum without your say-so. I’d gently encourage having someone you trust alongside you — it can help — but that’s your choice. The only time I’d ever need to share anything is if you were in danger, and I’d talk to you about it first."

"Can I ask a few things just to make sure you’re safe — who’s the father, how old is he, and was everything that happened something you wanted? … Thank you. I ask everyone this, it’s not about your decision."

"You’ve thought it through, and I’ll support your choice. I’ll refer you today to the service, or give you the number to book yourself — the earlier, the simpler the process, and they aim to offer the abortion within a week of seeing you. At seven weeks most people can take the tablets at home, or have a short procedure; they’ll go through the methods with you. Is there anything about continuing or other options you want to talk through, no pressure either way?"

"Afterwards, let’s sort reliable contraception so you’re in control going forward, and check for any infections. Here’s how to reach me and the service. If you get strong one-sided tummy pain, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or feel faint before your appointment, call 999 or go to A&E. And if you’re worried about anything — your health or your safety — come straight back."

f.learning: A 16-year-old requesting an abortion is an ethics-under-warmth station where the tone is the test: provide non-judgemental, patient-centred care with zero editorialising about abortion, her age or her decision, centring her autonomy whatever your private views. Assess and affirm competence — at 16 she is presumed able to consent to her own treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8), and Gillick competence is the test for under-16s (the Fraser guidelines apply only to contraception advice) — so answer her fear ("am I too young?") clearly: she can decide without parental consent if competent. Respect confidentiality, which is hers: encourage but do not force involving a parent or trusted adult, and explain that confidentiality is breached only for a serious safeguarding/risk concern, proportionately and ideally with her knowledge — this builds the trust that makes care possible. Crucially, weave in a safeguarding screen sensitively — the father’s identity and age (an adult or large age gap raises child-sexual-exploitation/abuse concern), whether sex was consensual, coercion/CSE/grooming indicators, and any pressure about the pregnancy decision — not to block her choice but to ensure she is safe. Give balanced information on all options (continuing, adoption, abortion) without steering, refer promptly to abortion services or give the self-referral route (NICE NG140; time-critical, earlier is simpler; NICE QS199: the abortion offered within 1 week of assessment; early medical abortion at home up to 9 weeks 6 days), address contraception and STI screening, and safety-net for ectopic pregnancy; a doctor with a conscientious objection must not obstruct — tell her she can see another doctor and make sure she can access care without delay (GMC). The hidden agenda is fear of being judged, controlled or refused and fear of her mother; make her feel safe, believed and in control, weave in safeguarding without policing, and ensure she leaves with a clear plan and trust — never a moral lecture or a breach of confidence.

knowledge.guideline: Abortion Act 1967 · NICE NG140 (abortion care, 2019, updated May 2025) and QS199 (2021) · Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8 · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014)
knowledge.summary: At 16 she can consent to her own treatment, and her confidentiality is hers. Your job is warm, non-judgemental care, a sensitive safeguarding check, and a prompt referral, because abortion is time-critical and simpler when early.

points.t: Young people of 16 and 17 can consent to their own medical treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8), and capacity is assessed as for adults (Mental Capacity Act 2005). No parental consent is needed. Gillick competence is the test for under-16s; the Fraser guidelines are the narrower test for contraception advice [4].

She is entitled to confidentiality. Encourage, but do not require, involving a parent or trusted adult. Share information without consent only where there is a risk of serious harm, telling her first unless that would increase the risk [4].

points.h: Safeguarding is part of routine care
points.t: Anyone under 18 is a child for safeguarding purposes [5]. Ask about the partner’s age and power, consent, pressure, alcohol or drugs, gifts and secrecy. Abortion and sexual-health services use a structured CSE screen such as Spotting the Signs for all under-18s [6].

points.h: The legal ground and the process
points.t: Two registered medical practitioners must agree, in good faith, that a lawful ground is met — most commonly that continuing the pregnancy (under 24 weeks) carries greater risk to her physical or mental health than ending it [1]. The GP does not need to sign the form to refer.

Women can self-refer to abortion services [2]. Providers should offer the abortion within 1 week of assessment [2]. Early medical abortion, with both medicines taken at home, is available in England and Wales up to 9 weeks 6 days, so at about 7 weeks she has every option if seen promptly.

Discuss contraception, including long-acting methods that can be started at the time of the abortion [2], and offer STI testing. Give non-directive information on all options — continuing, adoption, abortion — without steering.

dg.d: Warm open question; removes the fear of a lecture; lets her state her decision in her own words.
Home situation, relationship with her mother, a possible trusted adult, school, and any pressure from anyone.
Gestation by dates, pain or bleeding (ectopic screen); STI testing offered; the service arranges any scan and further assessment.
Considers pressure or coercion over the decision, CSE indicators and home safety, as well as certainty of choice.
Ectopic pregnancy symptoms asked and safety-netted; exploitation or abuse screened and excluded as far as possible.
Early pregnancy of about 7 weeks in a competent 16-year-old with a clear, uncoerced request for abortion; no safeguarding concern identified today.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Non-directive options; same-day referral or self-referral; medical and surgical routes explained; confidentiality respected; trusted adult encouraged, not forced.
Contraception, including LARC at the time of the abortion; STI testing; emotional support.
Ectopic red flags; call back if the service does not make contact; safe contact route agreed; open door if her safety changes.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up “am I too young?”, “don’t tell my mum” and “it’s not like that”, and responds to each.
Idea: she may not be allowed to decide; concern: judgement, refusal and her mother finding out; expectation: confidential help to access abortion.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — being judged or refused, and her mum finding out; scared of "messing up" the process — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Erin, I’m Dr Lee. Thank you for getting in touch — it takes courage. Before anything else: no lecture, I promise. Tell me what’s going on.
model.why: Answers her fear of judgement in the first sentence

model.text: I’m pregnant. I did a test. I’ve thought about it loads and I want an abortion. Please don’t tell my mum. Am I too young to decide?

Let me answer that straight away: no, you’re not too young. At 16 the law says you can make decisions about your own treatment, as long as you understand them. And I won’t tell your mum without your say-so.
model.why: Affirms her legal right to consent at 16 and states confidentiality clearly

model.text: Really? I thought you’d have to ring her.

No. The only time I’d ever share something is if I was worried you were in serious danger — and even then I’d talk to you first. Can I ask you some questions so I can help properly, and then we’ll make a plan together?
model.why: Explains the limit of confidentiality honestly and sets the agenda

model.text: Okay.
When was the first day of your last period, roughly? And have you had any pain or bleeding?
model.why: Dates the pregnancy and screens for ectopic symptoms

model.text: About seven weeks ago, I think. No pain or bleeding.
Thanks. You’ve said you’ve thought about it a lot. How sure do you feel, and has anyone been pushing you one way or the other?
model.why: Checks certainty and screens for pressure over the decision

model.text: I’m sure. It’s my decision. Nobody’s making me.

That’s clear. I ask everyone under 18 a few questions about safety — it’s not about your decision. Can you tell me a bit about the person you got pregnant with? How old are they, and was everything that happened something you wanted?
model.why: Normalised safeguarding screen: partner’s age, consent

model.text: He’s around my age. Yeah, it was what I wanted. It’s not like that.
Thank you. And has anyone ever given you alcohol, drugs, money or gifts in connection with sex, or asked you to keep things secret? Do you feel safe at home?
model.why: Completes the CSE indicators and checks home safety without assuming

model.text: No, nothing like that. Home’s fine. Mum would just go mad.
It sounds like the thought of your mum finding out is weighing on you. What worries you most about today?
model.why: Follows the cue about her mother and elicits concerns

model.text: That someone would say no, or make me feel like a bad person. And her finding out.

Nobody here is going to make you feel like that. You’ve come for help, which is the right thing. Some people find it helps to have one trusted adult alongside them — your mum, or someone else. That’s entirely your choice. Is there anyone like that?
model.why: Validates, and encourages without forcing a supportive adult

model.text: Maybe. I’ll think about it.

I’ll support what you’ve decided. So you have the full picture, the options are continuing the pregnancy, adoption, or an abortion — and if you want to talk through any of them, now or later, I’m happy to. No pressure either way.
No, I want the abortion.

Then here’s how it works. The abortion service will see you, usually by phone or video first. At your stage there are two choices: tablets, which most people at seven weeks can take at home, or a short procedure. They’ll go through both. The earlier it’s done, the simpler it is.
model.why: Explains medical and surgical options and why timing matters

model.text: Will they tell my mum?

No. They also keep it confidential. Like me, they’ll ask some safety questions because you’re under 18 — that’s routine. And if you take the tablets, it’s best to have someone with you at home that day — someone you choose.
model.why: Answers the repeated fear directly and prepares her for the service’s own safeguarding check

model.text: I’d like to refer you today, or I can give you the number to book yourself — whichever you prefer. They aim to offer the abortion within a week of seeing you.
model.why: Prompt referral, with self-referral as an option

model.text: Can you do it? I don’t want to mess it up.
Of course. I’ll do it today. What’s the safest way for them and me to contact you — your own mobile? Is it okay to leave a message?
model.why: Arranges a safe, confidential contact route

model.text: My mobile. Text is best.

Two more things, when you’re ready. Contraception — the service can start a long-acting method, like the implant or a coil, at the same time, so you’re in control afterwards. And a free, confidential check for infections. Would you like either?
model.why: Contraception, including LARC at the time of abortion, and STI testing

model.text: Yeah, the implant maybe. And the test is fine.

If before your appointment you get strong pain on one side of your tummy, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or you feel faint, that’s an emergency — call 999 or go to A&E. If the service hasn’t contacted you within a few days, ring me.
model.why: Ectopic red flags named plainly, with a clear fallback if the referral stalls

model.text: Okay.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what are you going to expect next?
The clinic texts me, they talk to me about tablets or the procedure, they ask some safety stuff, and I can get the implant. And it’s private.
Exactly. You’ve handled this really sensibly. And if anything changes — how you feel, or your safety — come straight back. Anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Affirms her, keeps the door open and shares the floor

social.t: Fear of a parent’s reaction is common. Explore who could support her (a relative, friend or school nurse) and practical needs such as someone at home on the day of a medical abortion.
Appointments can be arranged around school. Agree a safe way to contact her so that letters or calls do not reveal the pregnancy at home.

legal.t: Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8 lets a 16-year-old consent to treatment; the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies from 16. Gillick competence (1985) is the test for under-16s.

Abortion Act 1967: two doctors must agree in good faith that a lawful ground is met. Since the Crime and Policing Act 2026 (s241, in force 29 April 2026), a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy commits no offence under the abortion laws in England and Wales.

Under 18 is a child (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026). Share information if there are signs of abuse or exploitation, such as a large age or power gap, coercion, or gifts, drugs or alcohol linked to sex (GMC 0–18 years).

professional.t: A doctor with a conscientious objection must not express disapproval or obstruct access, must tell her she can see another doctor, and must make sure she can get care without delay (GMC Personal beliefs and medical practice). Referral is not participation in the abortion.
Record competence, her wishes about confidentiality, the safeguarding questions and answers, the referral and the safety-net.

community.t: NHS-funded abortion providers accept self-referral by phone or online; young people’s sexual-health services (for example Brook) offer contraception, STI testing and counselling.

redFlags: Unilateral abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, bleeding or fainting — possible ectopic pregnancy, same-day assessment
Partner much older or in a position of trust, coercion, gifts, drugs or alcohol linked to sex, secrecy — safeguarding concern
Pressure from anyone to continue or end the pregnancy
psychosocial: Home situation and her relationship with her mother
Who could support her; school; practical arrangements for the day
Emotional state and certainty of decision
ice: Idea: “Am I even allowed to decide this at 16?”
Concern: being judged, being refused, and her mum finding out
Expectation: confidential, no-lecture help to get an abortion

playbook.diagnosis: “You’re about seven weeks pregnant, you’ve made a clear decision, and you’re old enough to make it. My job is to get you seen quickly and safely, and to keep it confidential.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “At 16 the law treats you like an adult for decisions about your own treatment. You don’t need anyone’s permission — you just need to understand what you’re agreeing to, and you clearly do.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried someone would say no or make you feel bad. Nobody here will do that, and your mum won’t be told unless you choose to tell her.”
management.psychosocial: Offer, never force, a trusted adult; plan around school; agree a safe contact method; prepare her for the provider’s routine safety questions.
sharedPlan: Non-directive options; referral today (or self-referral) to the abortion service
Medical abortion at home (to 9 weeks 6 days) or surgical, chosen with the provider
Contraception including LARC at the time of abortion; STI testing
safetyNet: One-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or fainting — 999 or A&E
Contact the practice if the service has not been in touch within a few days, or if her safety changes

pitfalls.intro: Examiners are not testing your views on abortion. They are testing whether a frightened 16-year-old leaves with her rights explained, her safety checked, and a referral made — without feeling judged.

items.fail: Questioning a clear decision again and again, or adding personal comments about her age or the choice.
items.why: “Appeared judgemental” and “did not respect the patient’s autonomy”. The tone is the test here.
items.fix: Acknowledge the decision, offer non-directive information once, and move to the referral.

items.fail: Telling her she needs a parent’s consent, or applying the Fraser guidelines to abortion.
items.why: At 16 she can consent (Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8). Gillick is for under-16s; Fraser is for contraception advice.
items.fix: Answer her question plainly: “You can decide this yourself.”

items.fail: No safeguarding questions because “she’s 16 and it’s legal”.
items.why: Under 18 is a child for safeguarding. Missing a large age gap or coercion is a serious omission (GMC 0–18 years).
items.fix: Ask about the partner’s age, consent, pressure, gifts or drugs, and home safety — framed as routine.

items.fail: “Have a think and come back next week.”
items.why: Delay narrows options and adds risk. NICE NG140 supports self-referral and prompt access.
items.fix: Refer today or give the self-referral number, and tell her what to do if nobody calls.

items.fail: Forgetting ectopic red flags because the request is “only a referral”.
items.why: An unscanned early pregnancy may be ectopic; safety-netting is incomplete without it.
items.fix: Name one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, bleeding and fainting as reasons for 999 or A&E.

items.fail: Ending without contraception, STI testing or a safe way to contact her.
items.why: “Management plan insufficiently developed”; a letter to the family home could breach her confidentiality.
items.fix: Offer LARC at the time of abortion and STI testing, and agree how she wants to be contacted.

Gestation, pain or bleeding, certainty of decision, pressure from anyone, partner’s age, consent, CSE indicators, home safety.
Fear of judgement, refusal and her mother. Offer (never force) a trusted adult.
Non-directive options. Medical at home or surgical. Refer today or self-refer; contraception including LARC; STI testing.
Ectopic red flags, what to do if the service doesn’t call, safe contact route, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Moralises or steers; says she needs a parent’s consent or must tell her mum; skips the safeguarding questions or turns them into an interrogation; delays referral “to think about it”; no ectopic safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Non-judgemental; confirms she can consent at 16 and that the consultation is confidential; asks about partner’s age and consent; gives options and refers promptly; mentions contraception and STI testing; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: safeguarding questions framed as routine for every under-18; explains confidentiality’s limit honestly; agrees a safe contact route; prepares her for the service’s own safety check; offers LARC at the time of abortion; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.instead: “You’ve clearly thought about this. Is there anything about the options you’d like to talk through — no pressure either way?”
avoid.why: Repeated questioning of a clear decision reads as judgement and steering.

SCA_MODELS.why: Answers the repeated fear directly and prepares her for the service’s own safeguarding check

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d like to refer you today, or I can give you the number to book yourself — whichever you prefer. They aim to offer the abortion within a week of seeing you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Prompt referral, with self-referral as an option

SCA_MODELS.text: Can you do it? I don’t want to mess it up.
Of course. I’ll do it today. What’s the safest way for them and me to contact you — your own mobile? Is it okay to leave a message?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges a safe, confidential contact route

SCA_MODELS.text: My mobile. Text is best.

Two more things, when you’re ready. Contraception — the service can start a long-acting method, like the implant or a coil, at the same time, so you’re in control afterwards. And a free, confidential check for infections. Would you like either?
SCA_MODELS.why: Contraception, including LARC at the time of abortion, and STI testing

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, the implant maybe. And the test is fine.

If before your appointment you get strong pain on one side of your tummy, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or you feel faint, that’s an emergency — call 999 or go to A&E. If the service hasn’t contacted you within a few days, ring me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Ectopic red flags named plainly, with a clear fallback if the referral stalls

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what are you going to expect next?
The clinic texts me, they talk to me about tablets or the procedure, they ask some safety stuff, and I can get the implant. And it’s private.
Exactly. You’ve handled this really sensibly. And if anything changes — how you feel, or your safety — come straight back. Anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms her, keeps the door open and shares the floor

SCA_STEM.name: Erin Doyle
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Positive home pregnancy test. Approximately 7 weeks pregnant by her own dates. Attending alone.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation requested: “I need help with a pregnancy and I don’t want my mum told.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Abortion Act 1967 · NICE NG140 (abortion care, 2019, updated May 2025) and QS199 (2021) · Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8 · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: At 16 she can consent to her own treatment, and her confidentiality is hers. Your job is warm, non-judgemental care, a sensitive safeguarding check, and a prompt referral, because abortion is time-critical and simpler when early.

points.t: Young people of 16 and 17 can consent to their own medical treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8), and capacity is assessed as for adults (Mental Capacity Act 2005). No parental consent is needed. Gillick competence is the test for under-16s; the Fraser guidelines are the narrower test for contraception advice [4].

She is entitled to confidentiality. Encourage, but do not require, involving a parent or trusted adult. Share information without consent only where there is a risk of serious harm, telling her first unless that would increase the risk [4].

points.h: Safeguarding is part of routine care
points.t: Anyone under 18 is a child for safeguarding purposes [5]. Ask about the partner’s age and power, consent, pressure, alcohol or drugs, gifts and secrecy. Abortion and sexual-health services use a structured CSE screen such as Spotting the Signs for all under-18s [6].

points.h: The legal ground and the process
points.t: Two registered medical practitioners must agree, in good faith, that a lawful ground is met — most commonly that continuing the pregnancy (under 24 weeks) carries greater risk to her physical or mental health than ending it [1]. The GP does not need to sign the form to refer.

Women can self-refer to abortion services [2]. Providers should offer the abortion within 1 week of assessment [2]. Early medical abortion, with both medicines taken at home, is available in England and Wales up to 9 weeks 6 days, so at about 7 weeks she has every option if seen promptly.

Discuss contraception, including long-acting methods that can be started at the time of the abortion [2], and offer STI testing. Give non-directive information on all options — continuing, adoption, abortion — without steering.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Warm open question; removes the fear of a lecture; lets her state her decision in her own words.
Home situation, relationship with her mother, a possible trusted adult, school, and any pressure from anyone.
Picks up “am I too young?”, “don’t tell my mum” and “it’s not like that”, and responds to each.
Idea: she may not be allowed to decide; concern: judgement, refusal and her mother finding out; expectation: confidential help to access abortion.
Gestation by dates, pain or bleeding (ectopic screen); STI testing offered; the service arranges any scan and further assessment.
Considers pressure or coercion over the decision, CSE indicators and home safety, as well as certainty of choice.
Ectopic pregnancy symptoms asked and safety-netted; exploitation or abuse screened and excluded as far as possible.
Early pregnancy of about 7 weeks in a competent 16-year-old with a clear, uncoerced request for abortion; no safeguarding concern identified today.
Non-directive options; same-day referral or self-referral; medical and surgical routes explained; confidentiality respected; trusted adult encouraged, not forced.
Contraception, including LARC at the time of the abortion; STI testing; emotional support.
Ectopic red flags; call back if the service does not make contact; safe contact route agreed; open door if her safety changes.

social.t: Fear of a parent’s reaction is common. Explore who could support her (a relative, friend or school nurse) and practical needs such as someone at home on the day of a medical abortion.
Appointments can be arranged around school. Agree a safe way to contact her so that letters or calls do not reveal the pregnancy at home.

legal.t: Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8 lets a 16-year-old consent to treatment; the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies from 16. Gillick competence (1985) is the test for under-16s.

Abortion Act 1967: two doctors must agree in good faith that a lawful ground is met. Since the Crime and Policing Act 2026 (s241, in force 29 April 2026), a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy commits no offence under the abortion laws in England and Wales.

Under 18 is a child (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026). Share information if there are signs of abuse or exploitation, such as a large age or power gap, coercion, or gifts, drugs or alcohol linked to sex (GMC 0–18 years).

professional.t: A doctor with a conscientious objection must not express disapproval or obstruct access, must tell her she can see another doctor, and must make sure she can get care without delay (GMC Personal beliefs and medical practice). Referral is not participation in the abortion.
Record competence, her wishes about confidentiality, the safeguarding questions and answers, the referral and the safety-net.

community.t: NHS-funded abortion providers accept self-referral by phone or online; young people’s sexual-health services (for example Brook) offer contraception, STI testing and counselling.

redFlags: Unilateral abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, bleeding or fainting — possible ectopic pregnancy, same-day assessment
Partner much older or in a position of trust, coercion, gifts, drugs or alcohol linked to sex, secrecy — safeguarding concern
Pressure from anyone to continue or end the pregnancy
psychosocial: Home situation and her relationship with her mother
Who could support her; school; practical arrangements for the day
Emotional state and certainty of decision
ice: Idea: “Am I even allowed to decide this at 16?”
Concern: being judged, being refused, and her mum finding out
Expectation: confidential, no-lecture help to get an abortion

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’re about seven weeks pregnant, you’ve made a clear decision, and you’re old enough to make it. My job is to get you seen quickly and safely, and to keep it confidential.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “At 16 the law treats you like an adult for decisions about your own treatment. You don’t need anyone’s permission — you just need to understand what you’re agreeing to, and you clearly do.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried someone would say no or make you feel bad. Nobody here will do that, and your mum won’t be told unless you choose to tell her.”
management.psychosocial: Offer, never force, a trusted adult; plan around school; agree a safe contact method; prepare her for the provider’s routine safety questions.
sharedPlan: Non-directive options; referral today (or self-referral) to the abortion service
Medical abortion at home (to 9 weeks 6 days) or surgical, chosen with the provider
Contraception including LARC at the time of abortion; STI testing
safetyNet: One-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or fainting — 999 or A&E
Contact the practice if the service has not been in touch within a few days, or if her safety changes

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Examiners are not testing your views on abortion. They are testing whether a frightened 16-year-old leaves with her rights explained, her safety checked, and a referral made — without feeling judged.

items.fail: Questioning a clear decision again and again, or adding personal comments about her age or the choice.
items.why: “Appeared judgemental” and “did not respect the patient’s autonomy”. The tone is the test here.
items.fix: Acknowledge the decision, offer non-directive information once, and move to the referral.

items.fail: Telling her she needs a parent’s consent, or applying the Fraser guidelines to abortion.
items.why: At 16 she can consent (Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8). Gillick is for under-16s; Fraser is for contraception advice.
items.fix: Answer her question plainly: “You can decide this yourself.”

items.fail: No safeguarding questions because “she’s 16 and it’s legal”.
items.why: Under 18 is a child for safeguarding. Missing a large age gap or coercion is a serious omission (GMC 0–18 years).
items.fix: Ask about the partner’s age, consent, pressure, gifts or drugs, and home safety — framed as routine.

items.fail: “Have a think and come back next week.”
items.why: Delay narrows options and adds risk. NICE NG140 supports self-referral and prompt access.
items.fix: Refer today or give the self-referral number, and tell her what to do if nobody calls.

items.fail: Forgetting ectopic red flags because the request is “only a referral”.
items.why: An unscanned early pregnancy may be ectopic; safety-netting is incomplete without it.
items.fix: Name one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, bleeding and fainting as reasons for 999 or A&E.

items.fail: Ending without contraception, STI testing or a safe way to contact her.
items.why: “Management plan insufficiently developed”; a letter to the family home could breach her confidentiality.
items.fix: Offer LARC at the time of abortion and STI testing, and agree how she wants to be contacted.
